items.question: A utility's field-engineer assistant places two services in the request path: an input redaction service that strips customer identifiers before the model call, and an output policy classifier after it. Last week the classifier service itself became unavailable and, because the client treats a classifier error as a request error, the assistant was down for 90 minutes. The product owner has asked for that never to happen again. How should the architect specify guardrail-unavailability behaviour?

options.A: Make both guardrails fail open on error and emit a high-priority alert to the on-call channel, so the assistant remains available whatever happens.
options.B: Fold both checks into the main model call as system-prompt instructions, removing the two network hops that can fail independently.
options.C: Cache each guardrail's verdict keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the content, so during an outage the cached verdicts keep serving requests.
options.D: Choose fail-open or fail-closed per guardrail by the harm of unchecked content, and give the fail-closed one redundancy and a restricted degraded mode.

items.question: An architect moves a content check so that it runs asynchronously after the response has already been returned to the user. What has changed about the control?

options.A: It becomes a detective control: it can no longer prevent exposure, only shorten it and trigger remediation.
options.B: It becomes fail-closed, because the response can now be retracted after the check returns its verdict.
options.C: Its false-positive rate falls, because the classifier now sees the complete response rather than a partially generated one.
options.D: It removes the need for a separate input-side check, since every generated output is still examined by the same classifier.

items.question: A transit authority's app uses Claude to turn raw signalling and incident feeds into a plain-language disruption explanation. During a major signal failure, traffic reaches roughly twenty times normal and the model path becomes unavailable; the underlying structured feed of line status and last incident notes is unaffected. What should the app do while the model path is down?

options.A: Show a service-unavailable message in the disruption section, with a retry button, until the model path recovers.
options.B: Queue the requests and push the generated explanations to users as notifications once the model path is healthy again.
options.C: Render the structured feed — line status and raw incident notes — with a notice that the plain-language summary is unavailable.
options.D: Serve the most recent successfully generated summary for each line from the CDN cache, since it came from the same model path.

items.question: Why must an idempotency key for a retryable write be generated by the caller before the first attempt rather than by the receiving service when the request arrives?

options.A: Only a key fixed before the first attempt arrives identical on every retry, letting the receiver recognise the same logical operation.
options.B: A key created by the receiver cannot be stored alongside the recorded response, so no deduplication record can be written.
options.C: Caller-supplied keys let the receiver skip re-authenticating subsequent attempts, which is what makes a retry storm cheap to absorb.
options.D: A key created on receipt would make the operation idempotent for reads only, since writes are deduplicated by their payload contents instead.

items.question: A B2B analytics vendor offers an "explain this dashboard" feature backed by Claude, served to all customers from one service with a fixed pool of 200 worker slots. Two enterprise customers began submitting explanations over 60-page board reports that occupy a slot for 40 to 90 seconds each. During their nightly batch windows the pool fills, the sub-second requests from around 300 smaller tenants queue behind them, and the vendor breached its availability objective for those tenants three nights running. The model endpoint itself has been healthy throughout. Which change addresses this?

options.A: Increase the shared pool from 200 to 600 worker slots so there is enough headroom for the nightly batch window and interactive traffic together.
options.B: Partition the pool into capacity classes with their own concurrency limits and admission control, so each class consumes only its own share.
options.C: Put a circuit breaker on the long-running request path so it opens and sheds those calls when their p95 latency crosses 60 seconds.
options.D: Route long report explanations to a cheaper, faster model tier so each one occupies a worker slot for a fraction of the current time.

items.question: A wealth manager's Claude assistant answers client questions in chat and escalates to a human adviser whenever a question touches product suitability. Advisers receive a notification reading "client needs help" plus a link to the transcript. Average handling time after an escalation is now longer than for a cold inbound call, clients repeat information they already gave the assistant, and two advisers have contradicted commitments the assistant made earlier in the same conversation. What should the escalation carry?

options.A: Escalate at the first mention of a product, so there is less accumulated context for the adviser to absorb before speaking to the client.
options.B: A model-generated paragraph summarising the conversation and the client's goal, so the adviser reads one screen instead of the full transcript.
options.C: Read access to the underlying request logs in the platform observability tool, so advisers can see exactly what the assistant was sent and what it returned.
options.D: A structured handoff record: the conversation, the assistant's commitments, the rule that fired, its draft position and open questions, and a case id.

items.question: A queue guarantees at-least-once delivery to a consumer that performs an external write. What property must the consumer's side effects have for the pipeline to behave effectively-once?

options.A: They must be idempotent, or deduplicated at the point of effect, so a repeated delivery leaves the same end state.
options.B: They must be acknowledged to the broker before processing begins, so the message can never be redelivered after a crash.
options.C: They must be applied in strict message order by a single-threaded consumer reading one partition at a time.
options.D: They must complete inside the broker's visibility timeout window, so no message is ever returned to the queue.

items.question: A team is designing a three-stage fallback chain for a customer-facing Claude feature: primary model call, then a secondary model call, then a deterministic templated response. Which TWO properties must hold for the chain to genuinely reduce the probability of total failure rather than relocate it? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Each stage must cost less per call than the one before it, so the chain sheds spend at the same rate it sheds quality.
options.B: A fallback stage must not share failure modes with the stage it covers — endpoint, credential, quota pool or upstream dependency.
options.C: Each stage must use the same prompt template as the primary, so their outputs stay directly comparable in evaluation.
options.D: Each stage must be exercised routinely against real traffic, so it is not run for the first time during the incident it exists for.
options.E: A stage must be entered only once the preceding stage has exhausted its full retry policy, including every backoff interval it defines.

items.question: A manufacturer's shop-floor assistant does three things for maintenance technicians: it maps a symptom description to a part number, it generates a step-by-step repair procedure as free text, and it summarises a machine's recent alarm history. Part numbers are validated against the parts master before display; procedures are followed directly by the technician with no second check; alarm history is already visible unformatted in the plant's existing control-system view. During a provider incident the team can sustain about a third of normal call volume and must decide what to keep. What is the right degradation plan?

options.A: Keep all three capabilities but move every call to the cheapest tier, stretching the available call budget across the full feature set.
options.B: Keep procedure generation, which technicians rate as the most valuable, and disable symptom-to-part mapping and alarm summarisation.
options.C: Keep symptom-to-part mapping, leave alarm history to the existing control-system view, and route procedure requests to the indexed manual.
options.D: Queue all three request types and serve them from the backlog as capacity is restored, so no technician request is lost.

items.question: A shipping line's berth-scheduling assistant makes roughly 30 model calls an hour, unevenly distributed. Its circuit breaker is configured to open when the error rate exceeds 50% over a rolling 10-second window. In practice the breaker flaps: a single failed call in an otherwise empty window trips it and sheds legitimate traffic, and separately it stayed closed through a 12-minute dependency outage on a quiet night shift while every call during that period failed slowly. How should the breaker be reconfigured?

options.A: Require a minimum observation count before evaluating the ratio, size the window to the arrival rate, and add a periodic probe for sparse traffic.
options.B: Raise the error-rate threshold from 50% to 90% so a single isolated failure in an otherwise quiet window no longer trips the breaker.
options.C: Shorten the rolling window from 10 seconds to 2 seconds so failures are detected sooner and the breaker opens faster during a real dependency outage.
options.D: Remove the breaker and rely on a 5-second per-call timeout with two bounded retries, which suits a service at this volume better.

items.question: A clinical genomics laboratory runs about 400 Claude-assisted variant-interpretation requests a day. Each one informs a clinical report and may be re-examined years later if a patient's diagnosis is revisited. The platform team applied the company's default observability configuration, which samples 1% of traces and retains them for seven days — a policy that works well for the high-volume web services it was written for. What should the architect specify instead?

options.A: Raise trace sampling to 100% for this service while keeping the standard seven-day retention that the platform default applies.
options.B: Keep the 1% sampling rate but extend retention on the sampled traces to match the clinical review horizon of several years.
options.C: Keep a durable case record of every request's inputs, prompt and model version, output and reviewer decision for the clinical review horizon.
options.D: Record only the outputs and the reviewer's decision, since the inputs can be reconstructed from the laboratory information system when needed.

items.question: An insurance-claims agent maintains a running case summary that it checkpoints after each step. One run has now failed and been automatically resumed four times. Each resume restarts from the latest checkpoint, whose summary contains a policy limit that the model fabricated during step three; every resume reads that figure and produces the same incorrect determination, and the repeated failures appear on the dashboard as transient errors. What should the engineer do next?

options.A: Raise the resume limit from four to ten and add jitter between attempts, so the run has more chances to complete on its own.
options.B: Stop the automatic resume, roll the run back to the checkpoint before step three, and re-derive the policy limit from the policy system.
options.C: Clear all checkpoints across every in-flight claims run and restart them from the beginning to guarantee no contaminated state remains.
options.D: Add an instruction to the system prompt forbidding the model from stating a policy limit it has not retrieved from the policy system, then resume.

items.question: In a resilience design, what distinguishes a bulkhead from a circuit breaker?

options.A: A bulkhead retries failed calls in a dedicated pool so retries do not compete with first attempts; a breaker decides how many are allowed.
options.B: A bulkhead applies only to read traffic and a breaker only to write traffic, so that writes are never lost during a dependency failure.
options.C: A bulkhead caps how long any single call may run; a breaker caps how many of them may run concurrently against one dependency.
options.D: A bulkhead partitions finite resources so one workload cannot consume another's capacity; a breaker stops calling a failing dependency.

items.question: A hotel group's trip-assistant agent fans out five tool calls in parallel — room availability, loyalty balance, ancillary pricing, weather and local events — and then composes a recommendation in a single turn with a 4-second conversational budget. During a partner incident, loyalty balance and ancillary pricing time out at 800ms while the other three return normally. The agent currently waits for all five results and fails the turn when any is missing. What should it do instead?

options.A: Compose from the tools that returned, pass each failed tool's status into the model's context, and have it state what it could not check.
options.B: Retry the two timed-out tools synchronously with one backoff before composing, so the recommendation still covers all five sources.
options.C: Substitute the most recent cached loyalty balance and ancillary prices for the two failed tools so the model receives a complete result set.
options.D: Compose from the three successful tools without telling the model the other two failed, since it will notice the absence and hedge accordingly.

items.question: A platform team is standardising a checkpoint format for resumable Claude agent runs across several products, all of which call side-effecting internal services. Which THREE properties should the standard require? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The checkpoint records the durable output and decision state of each completed step, addressable by a stable step identifier.
options.B: The checkpoint stores the complete raw message transcript, since fidelity of the conversation is what makes a resume correct.
options.C: The intent to perform a side-effecting step, together with its idempotency key, is committed before that side effect is issued.
options.D: The checkpoint write and the external tool call are committed inside a single database transaction so the two can never diverge.
options.E: The checkpoint carries the prompt template and tool-schema versions in force when it was written, so an incompatible resume is detected.

items.question: A retailer's returns assistant has an 1,800ms p95 end-to-end budget. The chain allocates 1,500ms to generation and 250ms to a mandatory output check that requires the complete response to be valid, leaving 50ms of headroom. When generation runs long, the client's 1,800ms cancellation fires after generation finishes but before the check completes, and the current implementation returns the ungated draft to the customer rather than nothing. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Raise the end-to-end p95 budget from 1,800ms to 2,200ms so the 250ms check has room to complete after a long generation.
options.B: Deadline generation at the budget minus the check's worst case, and fall back to a degraded response rather than return unchecked text.
options.C: Run the check concurrently with generation, streaming partial text into it, so it never contributes to the tail latency.
options.D: Cache check verdicts keyed by a hash of the response text so an identical response skips the 250ms check entirely.

items.question: A grocery wholesaler's Claude-backed order-query assistant kept answering normally for nine days after an index migration silently caused the retrieval tool to return zero rows for one large product category. Answers for that category were fluent and wrong. Throughout the nine days, end-to-end latency, HTTP error rate and token spend were all unchanged. Which TWO instrumented signals would have surfaced the problem within hours? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: p95 end-to-end latency, tracked per endpoint with an alert on any week-over-week change beyond ten percent.
options.B: HTTP 5xx rate on the assistant's public API, alerted whenever it crosses a one-percent threshold over five minutes.
options.C: The proportion of turns in which the retrieval tool returned zero results, tracked per product category.
options.D: Token spend per request, averaged daily and alerted on a week-over-week change of more than ten percent.
options.E: The proportion of answers produced with no supporting retrieved document attached, tracked as a quality proxy.

items.question: In an asynchronous Claude processing pipeline, what is the primary purpose of a dead-letter queue?

options.A: To hold in-flight messages during a planned deployment so that nothing is lost while the worker fleet restarts.
options.B: To collect low-priority requests so that they can be processed later on a cheaper tier during off-peak hours.
options.C: To move messages that have exhausted their retry policy out of the main flow, preserving them for inspection and replay.
options.D: To store model outputs that failed a quality check, so they can be reviewed and fed back into prompt improvement.

items.question: A legal-drafting product streams long clause drafts into the browser. Users on unstable connections lose the stream partway through; the client reconnects and re-issues the same request. The customer is charged for two generations, and the second draft frequently differs materially from the first, which confuses users who had already begun working from the visible portion. What is the right design?

options.A: Set the sampling temperature to zero so that a re-issued request reproduces exactly the same draft the user was already reading.
options.B: Buffer the full response server-side and deliver it as one payload once it is complete, so a mid-stream disconnect cannot lose a partial draft.
options.C: Have the client post back the text it already received and ask the model to continue the clause from exactly where the stream stopped.
options.D: Create the generation once as a server-side resource under a client-supplied id, persisted as it streams, so a reconnect resumes from the offset.

items.question: A logistics operator is specifying when its autonomous procurement agent must pause and obtain human approval before continuing a run. The agent negotiates and places replenishment orders against pre-approved suppliers. Which THREE conditions should force the gate? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The next action produces effects that the agent cannot reverse on its own authority once they have landed.
options.B: The action would exceed the run's pre-declared bound on spend, records touched or counterparties contacted.
options.C: The step consumed more input and output tokens than the rolling weekly median recorded for all other steps of its type.
options.D: The agent has replanned or looped more often than its normal trajectory profile, so it is outside tested behaviour.
options.E: The model's response contained a tool_use block rather than a plain-text reply addressed to the user.

items.question: A publisher's article-enrichment pipeline runs as an HTTP ingest service, then a message queue, then a Claude summarisation worker, then a second queue, then a fact-check worker, then a write to the content system. Every service emits well-formed traces with spans and timings, but when an article is enriched incorrectly no engineer can follow that one article through the pipeline, because each service opens a new root trace at its own entry point. What is the fix?

options.A: Correlate spans at query time in the tracing backend by joining on article id and overlapping timestamp ranges across the six services.
options.B: Propagate trace context in the message envelope so each consumer continues the existing trace, with the article id as a searchable attribute.
options.C: Have all six components write to one shared log stream on the central platform so their records for an article sit together.
options.D: Replace the queues with synchronous HTTP calls between the six services, so that trace context propagates automatically through the request headers.

items.question: A hotel-booking platform's Claude concierge has had its circuit breaker open for 40 minutes. The provider incident that opened it was resolved 10 minutes ago and other services on the same account are succeeding normally. The breaker's half-open probe replays the last request that failed before it opened: a long multi-tool request that is still failing, but for an unrelated reason — one partner tool it calls has been down all week. The single breaker covers both the model call and the partner tool. What should the engineer do next?

options.A: Shorten the open-state timer so the half-open probe is retried every 30 seconds rather than after the full cool-down period.
options.B: Disable the breaker for the concierge service entirely until the partner tool that has been down all week is restored.
options.C: Swap the captured request for a representative model probe, and give the model and the partner tool separate breakers.
options.D: Manually force the breaker closed and watch the error-rate panel for the next ten minutes to see whether it holds.

items.question: In a multi-step request path, what distinguishes a deadline from a timeout?

options.A: A timeout is enforced by the calling client, while a deadline is enforced by the downstream service that receives the call.
options.B: A timeout bounds one call; a deadline is an absolute time carried with the request that each step derives its remaining budget from.
options.C: A deadline applies only to synchronous request paths, while a timeout applies to asynchronous work items taken from a queue instead.
options.D: A deadline is simply the sum of the per-step timeouts configured along the chain, computed for it at deployment time.

items.question: A telehealth provider uses Claude to draft the post-consultation summary that the treating clinician then signs. Volume is 9,000 consultations a day, the clinician already reads and signs every note as part of an unchanged existing workflow, and the median edit is minor. The safety team has proposed inserting a mandatory review queue staffed by clinical safety officers before drafts reach the signing clinician; that queue could clear roughly 600 notes a day. How should the human review be designed?

options.A: Adopt the mandatory safety-officer gate and grow that team fifteen-fold until it can clear all 9,000 notes a day before signing.
options.B: Send only the notes the model flags as uncertain to a safety officer, and let the remainder go out without the clinician's signature.
options.C: Keep the signing clinician as the in-path control, and spend the safety officers' capacity on risk-stratified audit of signed notes.
options.D: Replace the clinician's review with an automated second-model check of each draft, freeing clinician time while keeping a check in the path.

items.question: An energy trading desk runs a Claude agent that proposes intraday power trades. The model emits a structured order payload and an execution adapter submits it to the exchange. A deterministic validator — instrument whitelist, size cap, price collar — exists as a tool, and the system prompt instructs the model to call it and submit only on a pass. Last Thursday a run submitted an order the validator would have rejected, because the model called the submit tool without calling validate first. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Strengthen the system prompt so the validate-then-submit sequence is stated as mandatory, reinforced with a worked example of the correct ordering.
options.B: Add a second Claude call that reviews each order payload against the instrument whitelist, size cap and price collar before submit runs.
options.C: Remove the submit tool and have a duty trader re-key the model's payload into the exchange front end before it goes to market.
options.D: Move the validator inside the execution adapter so it runs on every submission, leaving the tool exposed to the model only as advisory feedback.

items.question: Under sustained overload of a model dependency, why is shedding excess requests generally preferable to queueing them?

options.A: A queue that fills faster than it drains slows every request and fails them anyway; shedding fails a subset and keeps the rest inside budget.
options.B: Queues in front of a model call cannot be given a maximum depth, so any queueing design in front of one is unbounded in latency by construction.
options.C: Shedding avoids paying the inference cost of the requests that are dropped, which is the main argument for using it in an incident.
options.D: Queued requests are admitted behind the circuit breaker, so a queue prevents the breaker from protecting the dependency.

items.question: At 09:40 an account manager reports that customer records in the CRM are showing mangled legal entity names. A scheduled Claude data-quality agent that normalises company names is midway through its run; its log shows 1.2 million records already updated under a normalisation rule changed in this morning's deploy, and the run is continuing. The agent holds a write credential covering the whole CRM. The CRM maintains a per-field change log with previous values, retained 90 days. What should the on-call engineer do next?

options.A: Halt the run and revoke the agent's write credential, then scope which records and fields were touched from the change log before remediating.
options.B: Start a reverse run that re-normalises the 1.2 million affected records back to their original form using the same pipeline.
options.C: Restore the whole CRM from last night's snapshot backup, which is known to predate this morning's deploy of the rule.
options.D: Pause the run, add a validation rule to the normalisation step, and resume so the remaining records are processed correctly.

items.question: A team adds request hedging to a Claude-backed lookup: if the first call has not returned by the observed p95, a duplicate call is issued and whichever response arrives first is used. Which TWO conditions must hold for this to be safe in production? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The hedge must be routed to a different model tier from the original, so that the two attempts cannot fail for the same reason.
options.B: The operation must be free of side effects, or carry an idempotency key, because both calls may reach and complete at the dependency.
options.C: Hedging must improve the median latency by as much as it improves the tail, or the extra inference spend is not justified.
options.D: The hedge rate must be capped and suppressed when the dependency is degraded, so hedging cannot double the load during an incident.
options.E: The hedge must be issued at the same instant as the original request so that both attempts start from an identical point.

items.question: A request passes through three tiers — an edge service, an orchestrator, and a worker that calls the model. Each tier retries a failed call up to two further times, so up to three attempts per tier, and all three use exponential backoff with jitter. Which TWO statements about this configuration are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: In the worst case a single user request can produce as many as 27 separate calls to the model endpoint at the innermost tier.
options.B: Because every tier applies exponential backoff with jitter, the total retry load stays bounded by the sum of the per-tier retry counts.
options.C: A retry budget scoped to the whole request, decremented by every tier's attempt, bounds amplification that per-tier policies cannot.
options.D: The innermost tier receives the fewest attempts, because it sits furthest from the caller that initiated the request.
options.E: Retrying at every tier is safe as long as the model call itself is stateless, since a stateless call can always be repeated.

items.question: A rail operator's passenger-information assistant has a tested fallback that serves templated status text whenever the model path fails. Since it was added, the user-visible error rate has stayed near zero and no alert has fired in six weeks. A quarterly review then finds that the model path has been failing for 18% of requests for a month, so nearly a fifth of passengers have been receiving templated text instead of the assistant. Which monitoring change addresses this class of problem?

options.A: Lower the alert threshold on the user-visible error rate so smaller increases are caught.
options.B: Alert on the model path's p95 latency, since a degrading dependency will show as slower responses first.
options.C: Alert on fallback activation rate, both against an absolute threshold and against its own trend.
options.D: Add a synthetic check that calls the assistant once a minute and alerts if it returns an error.

items.question: A prompt change is 40 minutes into a rollout on a 5% canary cohort of a document-classification service. Automatic rollback is configured to fire when the cohort's schema-validation failure rate exceeds 10%. The canary is running at 8.2% against a baseline of 0.3%, so rollback has not fired. Every failed classification is routed to a manual queue that is now 4,000 items deep and growing. The on-call engineer is watching the dashboard. What should the engineer do next?

options.A: Wait for the failure rate to cross 10% so the automated rollback fires and produces its own audit record.
options.B: Expand the canary to 20% of traffic to obtain a statistically firmer estimate of the true failure rate.
options.C: Lower the automatic rollback threshold from 10% to 5% so the automation performs the rollback itself.
options.D: Roll the canary back manually now, and correct the rollback threshold once the service is stable again.

items.question: In a workflow where an agent performs several external writes across different systems, what is a compensating action?

options.A: A re-execution of the failed step under the same idempotency key, so the effect is applied exactly once at the sink.
options.B: A separate operation that reverses the business effect of a completed step that cannot be undone by a transaction rollback.
options.C: A degraded response returned to the caller explaining that one of the workflow's external steps could not complete.
options.D: An audit-log entry recording what the failed step would have written to the external system if it had succeeded.

items.question: A hospital pharmacy system routes Claude-proposed medication-order clarifications to a named pharmacist for approval before they are sent to the prescriber. Last month several proposals sat in the pending state for more than 30 hours because the assigned pharmacist was on leave, and nothing in the system noticed. Which THREE elements must the approval step's specification include? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: An explicit deadline by which the pharmacist's decision must be recorded against the proposal.
options.B: The model's raw confidence score for the proposal, presented as the pharmacist's primary decision aid.
options.C: The default outcome that applies when that deadline expires, and who is notified when it does.
options.D: Commitment of the approval record in the same database transaction as the model call that produced the proposal.
options.E: A named escalation tier that receives the item when the primary approver has not acted or is unavailable.

items.question: A charity's donation-receipt service consumes a queue; each message triggers a Claude-generated receipt letter and an email send, deduplicated against an idempotency key held in a cache with a 24-hour time to live. Messages that exhaust their retries land in a dead-letter queue, where they historically wait two to nine days until an engineer investigates and replays them. After last week's replay, 3,100 donors received a second receipt. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Tighten the operational commitment so dead-letter messages are always investigated and replayed within the 24-hour cache window.
options.B: Make deduplication durable against a per-donation record rather than a short-lived cache, so the guarantee has no expiry.
options.C: Raise the retry count and lengthen the backoff intervals so that far fewer messages reach the dead-letter queue at all.
options.D: Generate a fresh idempotency key when a dead-letter message is replayed, so the replay is processed cleanly as a new operation.

items.question: A service can answer either from its primary model path or from a degraded templated path. What must the response contract include?

options.A: An HTTP error status on the response, so that callers treat any degraded answer as a failed request and automatically retry it later.
options.B: Nothing beyond the normal payload; the contract should stay identical so that existing callers require no changes.
options.C: A Retry-After header on the response, so the caller can come back later for the full-quality model answer.
options.D: An indication of which path produced the response, so callers, caches and evaluation can tell degraded output from normal.

items.question: A media company serves two workloads from one account and one shared token-per-minute allocation: an overnight archive-tagging batch and a customer-facing interactive assistant. Twice this quarter the batch has overrun into the morning and consumed enough of the allocation that interactive requests were throttled for around an hour. Which TWO changes contain the impact of a future overrun? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Increase the account's overall token-per-minute allocation so both workloads fit even when they overlap at peak.
options.B: Give each workload its own credential and allocation, so the batch cannot draw from the interactive workload's share.
options.C: Have both workloads share one connection pool and one scheduler so that utilisation is smoothed across the hour.
options.D: Apply priority-based admission that defers or sheds batch requests first when the interactive workload nears its ceiling.
options.E: Disable retries on the interactive workload so that it consumes less of the shared token allocation each minute.

items.question: A contact-centre agent-assist tool streams suggested replies to advisers while they are on a call. It currently applies a single 20-second total timeout to the streaming request. Two problems recur: long but genuinely useful suggestions are cut off at 20 seconds, and when the stream stalls after the first few tokens the adviser watches a frozen partial suggestion for the remaining time before anything happens. What timeout design fits this workload?

options.A: Raise the total streaming timeout from 20 seconds to 45 so the long but genuinely useful suggestions can complete.
options.B: Lower the total streaming timeout from 20 seconds to 8 so that stalled streams are abandoned quickly on the adviser's screen.
options.C: Apply three bounds: a time-to-first-token limit, an inter-token stall limit, and an overall deadline for the whole response.
options.D: Stop streaming and return the completed suggestion in one response, keeping a single 20-second timeout on the whole call.

items.question: For a Claude-backed feature, what is a synthetic probe intended to detect that live-traffic metrics cannot?

options.A: Failures on paths current traffic is not exercising, and failures a fallback is masking from user-visible metrics.
options.B: Cost regressions introduced by a prompt change, before they appear on the monthly provider invoice or budget alert.
options.C: Whether the model's answers are factually correct for the specific questions that real users are asking today.
options.D: How close the account is to its allocated request and token ceilings during the busiest peak periods of the day.

items.question: An immigration-advice charity runs a Claude intake assistant that gathers a long case history over 30 to 50 minutes of conversation. Session state lives entirely in the browser and is sent back with each turn. Clients often use shared library computers or phones with unreliable connectivity, so a closed tab or dropped session loses the entire intake and the client must start again. Caseworkers report clients abandoning after a second loss. What should the architect change?

options.A: Extend the browser session timeout to several hours and warn the user with a countdown banner before it expires.
options.B: Have the assistant emit a running summary that the client can copy and paste back into a new session in order to resume.
options.C: Shorten the intake to the ten most important questions so that losing a session costs the client less time.
options.D: Persist the conversation and extracted case state server-side after each turn under a resumable session id.

items.question: A team documents its degraded mode entirely as "the model call is skipped". What is missing from that specification?

options.A: The per-request cost saving that the mode delivers for as long as it stays active in production.
options.B: What the user receives, which guarantees hold, how the mode is entered and exited, and how it is signalled.
options.C: Which on-call engineers hold the authority to enable and disable the mode during an incident.
options.D: The model tier that would otherwise have served each request had the degraded mode not been active at the time.

items.question: In the design of an automated decision system, what distinguishes a human in the loop from a human on the loop?

options.A: A human in the loop reviews outcomes after they occur; a human on the loop reviews each proposal before it is acted upon.
options.B: A human in the loop curates the training and evaluation data; a human on the loop monitors production dashboards and metrics.
options.C: A human in the loop must decide before the action proceeds; a human on the loop supervises the autonomous system and can halt it.
options.D: A human in the loop implies a synchronous review interface, while a human on the loop implies an asynchronous batch one.

items.question: A supermarket chain's Claude agent reads supplier cost notifications and produces proposed shelf-price changes. For three weeks it has written proposals to a file that a pricing analyst applies by hand, and agreement between agent and analyst is 96%. The team intends to enable direct writes at Monday's release. The pricing system has no per-run scope control, so the agent's credential would cover all 40,000 stocked lines, and shelf prices are visible to customers and to the trading standards regime. What should the team do before Monday?

options.A: Enable direct writes as planned, since three weeks at 96% agreement across 40,000 lines is a stronger evidence base than most changes get.
options.B: Enable direct writes only within a declared scope — one category, a bounded magnitude and a per-run cap — leaving the rest on the manual path.
options.C: Delay the release until measured agreement reaches 99% over a further month of shadow running, then enable direct writes everywhere.
options.D: Add a deterministic rule that blocks any single price change greater than 20% of the current shelf price, and enable direct writes as planned.

items.question: An architect is defining the error taxonomy every service in the company will use when calling Claude, so that retry, alerting and fallback behaviour can be standardised across teams. Which THREE classes must be distinguished because each demands different handling? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Transient infrastructure failures such as connection timeouts and overload responses, which may well succeed on a later attempt.
options.B: Failures grouped by which team owns the calling service, so that alerts are routed automatically to the right on-call rotation for that team's service.
options.C: Malformed-request failures such as invalid parameters or oversized input, which fail identically on every attempt until the request changes.
options.D: Failures grouped by the model tier in use, since each tier is held to fail in characteristically different ways at load.
options.E: Calls that succeeded but whose content fails a downstream contract — a schema mismatch or truncation at the token limit — needing regeneration.

items.question: An airline's baggage-policy assistant answers passenger questions from a policy corpus that the revenue team revises roughly twice a year. The team is choosing a fallback for model-path outages. A sister team that runs the live-disruption assistant has told them that serving cached answers during an outage is always the wrong call, having learned it the hard way during a signalling incident. What fallback fits the baggage assistant?

options.A: Serve cached answers keyed by question intent, labelled with the policy version, and invalidate the cache whenever the corpus is revised.
options.B: Adopt the sister team's blanket rule and show a service-unavailable message for that topic rather than serving any cached content at all.
options.C: Serve the underlying conditions-of-carriage document directly to the passenger for the baggage topic they asked about.
options.D: Fall back to a lower-capability model reading the same policy corpus, so that an answer is still generated fresh each time.

items.question: A government procurement unit runs a Claude tool that summarises supplier tender submissions arriving through a scanned-document pipeline. About 3% of pages come out of OCR corrupted — columns dropped, text interleaved, tables truncated. The model summarises those pages fluently and without hesitation, and two such summaries reached evaluation panels before anyone noticed. The output policy check runs after the model and passes every time, because the summaries are well formed. What is the correct change?

options.A: Extend the output policy check so that it flags summaries that were produced from corrupted or interleaved OCR source text.
options.B: Instruct the model in its system prompt to state whenever its source text appears unreadable and to decline to summarise those pages.
options.C: Re-run OCR at higher resolution and quality settings across the whole tender corpus to bring the 3% corruption rate down.
options.D: Gate content before the prompt: score each page for OCR confidence, exclude failures, and name the unread pages in the summary.

items.question: A facilities-management agent handles emergency callouts in three steps: book a contractor through the supplier portal, write a purchase order into the finance system, notify the site manager. A worker was evicted after a successful contractor booking but before the purchase-order write. The message is back on the queue and will be redelivered within minutes. The supplier portal accepts an idempotency header, but the current code generates a fresh value on each attempt, and the portal exposes a booking lookup by site and time window. What should the engineer do next?

options.A: Let the redelivery proceed, on the basis that a duplicate contractor booking costs less than a missed emergency callout.
options.B: Deploy a fix that derives the idempotency key from the callout identity, so the redelivery is deduplicated by the portal.
options.C: Pause the consumer, query the portal to establish whether the booking exists, and resume the workflow from the purchase-order step.
options.D: Delete the message from the queue outright so that no duplicate contractor booking can be created on redelivery.

items.question: What does it mean for a service to be statically stable during the failure of a dependency?

options.A: It retries the failed dependency continuously, holding incoming requests in memory until the dependency has recovered.
options.B: It continues operating on the last known good state it already holds, without a new answer from the dependency.
options.C: It rejects all incoming requests immediately so that no load at all accumulates against the failed dependency.
options.D: It switches automatically to a warm standby replica of the dependency running in a second region on failure.

items.question: A customs brokerage runs a Claude step that proposes tariff classifications, which a licensed broker accepts or edits before the entry is filed. The system logs the model's proposal and the final filed classification. Six months in, the team wants to use broker corrections both to improve the system and to answer audit questions about why a classification changed. It finds it can report that 11% of proposals were edited, but not in what way or for what reason. What should the architect change?

options.A: Extend log retention from six months to three years so that more decision history is available for analysis and audit.
options.B: Ask brokers to record a free-text note in the team's existing ticketing system whenever they edit a proposed classification.
options.C: Have a nightly model job compare each proposal with the final filed value and infer the reason the broker made the edit.
options.D: Capture the review as an event: the proposal, the final value, the structured diff, a broker reason code and the request id.

items.question: An in-path output guardrail is adding materially to p95 latency on a customer-facing Claude feature, and the product owner wants the time back. Which TWO changes reduce the guardrail's latency contribution while keeping it a preventive control? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Apply the guardrail to a randomly sampled 10% of responses and let the remaining 90% through to customers unchecked.
options.B: Evaluate the guardrail on the smallest unit it can validly assess, so checking overlaps generation rather than following it.
options.C: Move the guardrail to run after delivery and retract any response in the widget that subsequently fails the check.
options.D: Run the guardrail's independent sub-checks concurrently rather than chained, so the cost is the slowest check not their sum.
options.E: Cache guardrail verdicts keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the response text so that repeated responses skip the check entirely.

items.question: A semiconductor fab runs a Claude yield-analysis agent that queries process databases and iterates until it can explain a wafer excursion. Each tool call carries a 30-second timeout and each model call a 60-second timeout. Process engineers expect an answer within about 10 minutes. Last week one run executed 46 steps over 68 minutes, held a database connection throughout, and eventually returned an answer nobody was still waiting for. What should the architect change?

options.A: Bound the run with a wall-clock deadline and step ceiling in the orchestrator, and return the best partial analysis when the budget is spent.
options.B: Reduce the per-tool timeout from 30 to 10 seconds and the per-model timeout from 60 to 30 seconds so each step is far cheaper.
options.C: Instruct the agent in its system prompt to complete the analysis within ten minutes and stop once it has sufficient evidence.
options.D: Move the agent to a faster model tier so that each of its steps completes in considerably less wall-clock time.

items.question: Which question most directly measures the blast radius of a change to a prompt template shared across many customers?

options.A: How many additional input tokens the change adds to every request that uses the template.
options.B: How many senior engineers reviewed and approved the change before it was merged to the main branch.
options.C: What fraction of traffic, and which customers, the change can affect before it can be stopped.
options.D: How long the change took to author, review and test in staging before it was released.

items.question: A distributor wants to let its Claude replenishment agent run unattended overnight, placing stock orders with suppliers while nobody is on shift. Which THREE conditions must hold before that is enabled? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The run carries hard limits on actions, spend and wall-clock time, enforced by the orchestrator rather than the agent's reasoning.
options.B: Every side-effecting step either has a defined compensating action or is deferred to the morning approval queue for a human.
options.C: The overnight run uses the same prompt template and tool set as the supervised daytime path, so that behaviour stays consistent between them.
options.D: Completion is asserted positively: a run that ends without its terminal state raises an alert rather than being silently absent.
options.E: The overnight run uses the highest-capability model tier available, since no human is on shift overnight to catch mistakes.

items.question: A broadband provider's self-service assistant streams its reply to the customer while it works. In the engineer-visit flow it streams "I've scheduled your engineer visit for Thursday morning" and then calls the scheduling tool, which sometimes fails because the slot was taken in the interim. By then the customer has read the confirmation, and text already delivered to the widget cannot be withdrawn. What is the right change?

options.A: Append a clearly worded correction message to the end of the conversation whenever the scheduling tool subsequently fails.
options.B: Restructure the turn so the scheduling call resolves before any commitment is streamed, generating the confirmation from its actual result.
options.C: Retry the scheduling tool with backoff until a Thursday morning slot is booked, so the streamed confirmation becomes true.
options.D: Pre-reserve a Thursday slot at the start of any conversation that mentions an engineer visit, releasing it if the customer does not confirm.

items.question: What distinguishes graceful degradation from failover?

options.A: Failover is always automatic, whereas graceful degradation must always be initiated manually by an on-call operator.
options.B: Failover applies only to stateless services, while graceful degradation applies only to stateful ones such as caches.
options.C: Failover handles infrastructure failures, while graceful degradation handles model quality regressions and gradual output drift instead.
options.D: Failover moves the workload to an equivalent replacement and preserves the contract; degradation reduces it to surviving capacity.

items.question: A retail-energy company has six product teams building Claude features and expects four more next year. Each team wraps the SDK in its own helper, and the helpers differ in what they record: two log the rendered prompt, one logs only the output, none records the stop reason, and correlation identifiers are named differently in each. A platform engineer has been given time to fix this before the estate grows. Which approach gives the most durable result?

options.A: Provide one shared client library every team calls, emitting the standard fields — correlation id, prompt version, stop reason, usage — on each call.
options.B: Publish a company-wide logging standard and review each of the six teams' implementations against it in the architecture forum.
options.C: Deploy a sidecar that captures request and response bodies at the network layer for every service, so that nothing depends on application code.
options.D: Have each of the six teams add the missing telemetry fields to its own SDK wrapper before that team's next scheduled release.

items.question: A service protects its model dependency with a circuit breaker and also has a deterministic fallback path. Which TWO statements about how the two should interact are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: While the breaker is open, requests are served by the fallback with no attempt on the primary — fast failure is what the breaker supplies.
options.B: The fallback should sit behind the same breaker instance, so both paths are shed together whenever the dependency is unhealthy.
options.C: Half-open probes should be served from the fallback, so that no user at all is exposed to a request against a dependency that may not have recovered.
options.D: The fallback must be capacity-planned for the full request volume, because an open breaker directs 100% of traffic straight to it.
options.E: The breaker should close as soon as the fallback's own error rate rises, since that shows the fallback cannot cope with the load.

items.question: An online marketplace onboards about 5,000 new sellers a week. A Claude step assesses each application against listing policy, and the risk team then reviews every case before the seller may list; the median wait is 26 hours and is the largest single cause of onboarding drop-off. The risk team has depth capacity for roughly 900 cases a week. Sellers can be suspended and their listings removed at any time, and the marketplace already does this routinely with same-day effect. How should the review be positioned?

options.A: Keep the synchronous gate and grow the risk team fivefold until it can review all 5,000 cases a week within a few hours.
options.B: Auto-approve the applications the model scores as confident and hold the remainder in the existing synchronous review queue.
options.C: Let sellers list immediately on the model's assessment, and run human review asynchronously against a risk-ranked queue.
options.D: Let all sellers list immediately and retire the human review step entirely, relying on post-listing monitoring and buyer reports.

items.question: A pharmaceutical distributor is preparing to give a Claude agent write access to its product master-data system so it can correct records at scale. The system has no native per-run scoping and its records feed order fulfilment. Which THREE controls bound the blast radius of a bad run? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Each run declares a scope — one product family or one date range — and the tool layer rejects writes outside it.
options.B: Operations above a size threshold produce a preview diff that must be approved before any write is executed at all.
options.C: The agent runs on a higher-capability model tier so that it makes materially fewer mistakes on the records in the first place.
options.D: A kill switch revokes the agent's write credential immediately, without requiring a deploy or any code change.
options.E: The agent records a natural-language justification for every write that it performs, retained for later audit review.
